1.pericope_label: And the Lord called unto Moses, and spake unto him out of the tabernacle of the congregation, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, If any man of you bring an offering unto the Lord, ye shall bring your offering of the cattle, even of the herd, and of the flock.

schools.summary: Begin with the book before the verse. The third book is headed in the original from its opening word, while the Septuagint and Vulgate call it Leviticus from the leading character of its contents, probably with some reference to the titles current among the Rabbins, law of the priests and law-book of sacrificial offerings. Say what it does: it carries on to its completion the giving of the law at Sinai which commenced at the twenty-fifth chapter of the previous book, by which the covenant constitution was firmly established, and it contains the laws regulating the relation of Israel to its God, both the principles on which covenant fellowship depended and the directions for the sanctification of the covenant people; so that these laws might justly be described as the spiritual statute-book of Israel as the congregation of Jehovah. Then correct the English of the opening clause. Render it rather, and he called unto Moses, and the Lord spake, and point out that the connection with what precedes is carried by the single Hebrew word and he called: at the end of the previous book the Lord showed his approbation of the completed tent by covering it with a cloud and filling it with his glory, and he who had so filled the sanctuary now calls out of it. Add the observation, already made by the ancient synagogue, that this unusual phrase serves as an introductory formula on the three occasions when a special communication was made to this lawgiver, from the burning bush, from the top of Sinai, and now from the tent of meeting. On the second verse, note that the directions for the sacrifices are not communicated in the first instance to the priests, to be taught by them to the people, but are addressed directly to the people themselves; and render the clause, from the cattle ye shall bring your offering, from the oxen and from the flock, so that if the offering is of quadrupeds, in contradistinction to the fowl allowed later in the chapter, it must be of oxen and of small cattle, that is, sheep and goats. Explain finally why the burnt offering is generally rendered by a word meaning wholly burnt, since the animal was all consumed upon the altar.

State your method before you begin, since these seven chapters treat generally of the sacrifices and much in them has passed away. Own that the use of many things here is gone and that the grounds of others are not understood, and content yourself with a brief summary, from which the reader may nevertheless perceive that whatever has been left to us of the legal sacrifices is even now profitable, provided we are not too curious. Let those who choose to hunt for allegories receive the praise they covet; the object is only to profit readers, and it will suffice to sum up briefly what is useful to be known. Then take the calling itself. Note that the verb may be rendered met him, and that the last letter of the word is written in a very small character, on which the Jews build several explanations: that God met Moses accidentally and unawares to him; that it respects the modesty of Moses, who lessened himself and got out of the way that the government might not be laid upon him; or that it marks the wonderful condescension of the Lord, whose throne is in heaven and who yet vouchsafed to dwell in a tabernacle and to call out of it. Observe that the word Lord is not in the first clause but supplied by the translators from the next, and record that the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem paraphrase it, the Word of the Lord called to Moses, by an articulate voice, though perhaps a still small one, which some think is the reason for the small letter. On the second verse, mark the limit of the address: to no other than the children of Israel was the law of sacrifices given, and not to the Gentiles. Then lay down the rule that governs the whole chapter. Three kinds are enumerated, of the herd, of the flocks and of fowls, the red heifer being a different and peculiar case. Only clean animals were chosen, and not even all clean animals, but only the domestic ones which allow themselves to be directed by the hand and will of men; for though deer and roes are sometimes tamed, God did not admit them to his altar. This was the first rule of obedience, that men should not offer promiscuously this or that victim. And freedom from blemish is required for two reasons: since the sacrifices were types of Christ, it behoved that in all of them should be represented that complete perfection of his by which the heavenly Father was to be propitiated; and the Israelites were reminded that all uncleanness was repudiated by God, lest his service should be polluted by their impurity.

Introduce the book at length, since the reader is beginning it. The Greek and Latin versions gave it the title Leviticus, retained in almost all the modern versions, because it treats principally of the laws and regulations of the Levites and priests; in Hebrew it is termed from its first word, and he called, which became the running title to the whole. Set out what it contains, the ceremonies of burnt sacrifices, meat, peace and sin offerings, the consecration of priests, and the three grand national festivals; note that it seems to contain little more than the history of the eight days of Aaron's consecration, though Usher supposed it covers a month; and refuse to guess further, since there are no data by which a chronological arrangement can be made and it would be useless to encumber the page with conjectures which, being uncertain, answer no end to the serious reader. Give the reading rule: as the law was our schoolmaster unto Christ, the whole sacrificial system was intended to point out that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and without that spiritual reference no interest can be excited by a perusal of the work. Then take the word for offering, from a root meaning to approach or draw near, signifying a gift by which a person had access unto God; and illuminate it from the universal custom of the east, that no man is permitted to approach the presence of a superior without a present, so that this is properly the introduction-offering, or offering of access. Define the terms exactly: the cattle are animals of the beeve kind, restrained by the word herd to the ox and heifer; the flock is sheep and goats, no other small clean quadruped ever having been offered. Observe that these are the very animals God commanded Abraham to offer, from which it is evident that God delivered to the patriarchs an epitome of the law afterwards given in detail. Then set the contrast with the heathen, among whom obscene fowls and ravenous beasts were offered according to the nature of their deities, horses to the Sun, wolves to Mars, asses to Priapus, swine to Ceres and dogs to Hecate, while here gross-feeding and ferocious animals are all excluded, as are birds of prey, and fish were not offered because they could not readily be brought to the tabernacle alive. Finally give the reasons for the variety of sacrifices: some acknowledged mercies desired or received, some satisfied for sin, some were mere exercises of devotion; the number suited the childish state of a people much addicted to outward rites, that they might have full employment of that kind in God's service and be kept from temptations to idolatry; and no one sort could have represented at once the several perfections of Christ, the various benefits of his death, and the several duties men owe.

Take four things for granted and then say why each matters. First, that people would be inclined to bring offerings to the Lord at all: the very light of nature directs man, some way or other, to do honour to his Maker and pay him homage as his Lord, and revealed religion supposes natural religion to be an ancient and early institution, since the fall had directed men to glorify God by sacrifice, which was an implicit acknowledgment of their having received all from God as creatures and forfeited all to him as sinners. Second, that provision must be made against invention: men are not to indulge their own fancies, nor become vain in their imaginations about their sacrifices, lest while they pretend to honour God they really dishonour him and do what is unworthy of him; everything is therefore directed to be done with due decorum, by a certain rule, so that the sacrifices might be significant both of the great sacrifice of atonement which Christ was to offer in the fulness of time, and of the spiritual sacrifices of acknowledgment which believers should offer daily. Third, that God gave these laws to Israel by Moses. He could have spoken them to the people himself, as he did the ten commandments, but they had desired he would no more speak to them so, and he had designed that Moses above all the prophets should be a type of Christ, by whom God would in these last days speak to us; by other prophets God sent messages to his people, but by Moses he gave them laws. Fourth, that he spoke out of the tabernacle. As soon as the shechinah had taken possession of its new habitation, in token of the acceptance of what was done, God talked with Moses from the mercy-seat while he attended at the door, hearing a voice only; and it is probable that he wrote what he heard at the time, to prevent any slip of memory in the rehearsal of it. The tabernacle was set up to be a place of communion, and there, where they performed their services to God, God revealed his will to them. Then make the contrast that governs the tone of the whole book. The Lord called Moses, not to come near, for under that dispensation even Moses must keep his distance, but to attend and hearken; and note that a letter less than ordinary in the Hebrew word for called intimates that God spoke in a still small voice. The moral law was given with terror from a burning mountain, in thunder and lightning; but the remedial law of sacrifice is given more gently from a mercy-seat, because that was typical of the grace of the gospel, which is the ministration of life and peace.

debates.question: Why is the last letter of the word for called written small?

sides.position: The Jewish explanations: that God met Moses unawares, that it marks his modesty in getting out of the way, or God's condescension in leaving heaven for a tent
That the voice was still and small — the remedial law of sacrifice given gently from a mercy-seat, where the moral law came with thunder from a burning mountain

debates.question: Why were these animals and no others appointed?

sides.position: Because they are clean and domestic, submitting to the hand of men; deer and roes are sometimes tamed and still refused the altar
Because they are the same God commanded Abraham to offer, the patriarchs having had an epitome of the law given later in detail
Either to bring the Egyptian deities into contempt, or as fittest representations of Christ and of Christians, or as the best and most common creatures

outliers.note: Alone states a method instead of an exposition, declining to expound what has passed out of use or what he does not understand, and leaving allegory to those who choose to hunt for it and may have the praise they covet.
Alone notes that this book's opening word is the same formula that introduces the three great communications to Moses — from the burning bush, from Sinai, and now from the tent of meeting.

3.pericope_label: If his offering be a burnt sacrifice of the herd, let him offer a male without blemish: he shall offer it of his own voluntary will at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation before the Lord. And he shall put his hand upon the head of the burnt offering; and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.

schools.summary: Set the burnt offering in its place in the scheme before expounding it. Having stated what is meant by the cattle, the directions now treat of the kinds of offering themselves, and first in order comes the burnt offering, divided into that from the beeves and that from the flock; the ox takes precedence because it is the more costly and more important sacrifice. Insist on the condition: it had to be without disease or blemish of any kind, since to offer a defective sacrifice was an insult and a deception, which is why the prophet cries, cursed be the deceiver which hath in his flock a male and voweth and sacrificeth unto the Lord a corrupt thing. Then correct the received rendering of the next clause, which is the crux of the verse. The whole passage is better read, at the entrance of the tent of meeting shall he offer it, that he may be accepted before the Lord; and the meaning is put beyond doubt by a later chapter where it is explicitly declared, ye shall offer for your acceptance a male without blemish of the beeves, of the sheep or of the goats, but whatsoever hath a blemish that ye shall not offer, for it shall not be acceptable for you. Remark that the phrase for your acceptance is used only in connection with burnt offerings and peace offerings, and never with sin offerings. On the laying on of hands, render it lay his hand, and observe that the ceremony was enjoined not only for burnt offerings but for peace offerings and sin offerings too, that is, in every case where the details of the ceremonial are minutely described, while no allusion is made to it wherever the description is condensed. Take the verb to imply a forcible pressure of the hand upon the head. Say what the gesture meant: the offerer indicated both the surrender of his ownership of the victim and the transfer to it of the feelings by which he was influenced in this act of dedication. Then add what is known of the practice: from the second Temple we know that the offerer himself laid both his hands between the two horns of the animal while it was alive, that no proxy could do it, and that if several offered one sacrifice each laid his hand separately, confessing his sins and saying, I have sinned, I have committed iniquity, I have transgressed and I have done this and this, but I repent before thee, and this is my atonement. Conclude on the atonement: because the imposition of hands, confession, repentance and prayer accompanied this sacrifice, and because these acts secure acceptance, an expiatory virtue is here ascribed to the burnt offering which belongs more especially to the sin and trespass offerings.

Explain the name from the Hebrew rather than from the ceremony. The word comes from a root which signifies to ascend or go up, because the victim was not only carried up to the altar by the priest, which was common to other sacrifices, but being burnt upon it ascended upwards in smoke and vapour; and the Greek name is a whole burnt offering, since all of it was consumed except the skin. Then read it typically, as of Christ's dolorous sufferings and death, in which he sustained the fire of divine wrath and his strength was dried up like a potsherd; and record that Jarchi says there were in the burnt offerings mysteries of future things. On the laying on of hands, gather what the Jewish authorities require, and do not smooth over their differences. The Targum of Jonathan says it was the right hand, but it is generally thought by the Jewish writers that both hands were laid on; so Ben Gersom and Aben Ezra, and Maimonides agrees, who says that he who lays on hands ought to lay on with all his strength, with both his hands upon the head of the beast, as the text says, upon the head of the burnt offering, not upon the neck nor upon the sides, and that there should be nothing between his hands and the beast. Add the further rule that it must be his own hand, and not the hand of his wife, nor of his servant, nor of his messenger. Note also that at the same time he made confession over the burnt offering, both of his sins committed against affirmative precepts and of those against negative ones. Then draw the conclusion the ceremony is for: by this action he owned that he had sinned, and deserved to die as the creature he brought was about to die, and that he expected the pardon of his sin through the death of the great sacrifice to come.

Begin by distinguishing this offering from the rest. It is strictly so called because it was to be all burnt, the skin excepted, for every sacrifice was burnt more or less; and it is the most important of all the sacrifices offered to God, called by the Greek version wholly consumed, which was not the case in any other offering. Then draw out what the totality signified: that the whole man, in whose stead the sacrifice was offered, was to be entirely offered or devoted to God's service; that the whole man did deserve to be utterly consumed, if God should deal severely with him; and that we are directed to serve the Lord with singleness of heart, and to be ready to offer to God even such sacrifices or services wherein we ourselves shall have no part or benefit. Take the two conditions in turn. A male, as being more perfect than the female and more truly representing Christ. Without blemish, to signify that God should be served with the best of every kind, that the man represented by these sacrifices should aim at all perfection of heart and life, that Christians shall one day attain to it, and that the holiness of Christ was spotless and complete. On the clause rendered of his own voluntary will, be candid about the difficulty. The Hebrew means rather to gain himself acceptance before the Lord, and all the versions appear to have understood the original words so, the connection in which they stand obviously requiring this meaning; but if the received translation be kept, the place speaks only of freewill offerings, such as were not prescribed by God to be offered in course but were offered by the voluntary devotion of any person, either by way of supplication for a mercy or by way of thanksgiving for a blessing received; and it may seem improper to restrain the rules given here to freewill offerings, since they were to be observed in the other offerings also. On the place, note that it was in the court near the door where the altar stood, for there it was to be sacrificed and there the people might behold the oblation; and read that as signifying that men can have no entrance, neither into the earthly tabernacle, the church, nor into the heavenly tabernacle of glory, but by Christ, who is the door. Finally, on the imposition of hands, say that both hands were used, and that by it the offerer signified that he willingly gave the victim to the Lord, that he judged himself worthy of the death it suffered in his stead, and that he laid his sins upon it with an eye to him upon whom God would lay the iniquity of us all, offering up himself together with it. Number what the gesture acknowledged, and then set the ancient world beside it: almost all the people of the earth had their burnt offerings and placed the greatest dependence on them, it being a general maxim through the heathen world that there was no other way to appease the incensed gods, so that they sometimes even offered human sacrifices, holding, as Caesar reports of the Gauls, that the divine will could not be appeased unless a life were rendered for a life.

Suppose a rich man who can afford it, and take the rules one by one as religiously to be observed. First, the beast must be a male, without blemish, and the best he had in his pasture: being designed purely for the honour of him that is infinitely perfect, it ought to be the most perfect in its kind, which signified the complete strength and purity that were in Christ the dying sacrifice, and the sincerity of heart and unblamableness of life that should be in Christians, who are presented to God as living sacrifices. But guard the application at once: literally, in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female, nor is any natural blemish in the body a bar to our acceptance with God, but only the moral defects and deformities introduced by sin into the soul. Second, the owner must offer it voluntarily, for what is done in religion so as to please God must be done by no other constraint than that of love, God accepting the willing people and the cheerful giver; though Ainsworth and others read the clause not as the principle but as the end of offering, let him offer it for his favourable acceptation before the Lord, and let his eye be fixed steadily on that end. Third, it must be offered at the door of the tabernacle, where the brazen altar stood, which sanctified the gift, and not elsewhere: at the door, as one unworthy to enter, acknowledging that there is no admission for a sinner into covenant and communion with God but by sacrifice, and at the tabernacle of the congregation, in token of his communion with the whole church of Israel even in this personal service. Fourth, the offerer must put his hand upon the head of his offering, both his hands, say the Jewish doctors, with all his might, between the horns of the beast. Say what the three things are that this signified: the transfer of all his right to and interest in the beast to God, actually and by a manual delivery; an acknowledgment that he deserved to die, and would have been willing to die if God had required it; and a dependence upon the sacrifice as an instituted type of the great sacrifice on which the iniquity of us all was to be laid. Add that some think the apostle means this rite by the doctrine of laying on of hands, which typified evangelical faith. And close on the scope of it: though the burnt offerings had not respect to any particular sin, as the sin offering had, yet they were to make atonement for sin in general, so that he who laid his hand on the head of a burnt offering was confessing that he had left undone what he ought to have done and done what he ought not to have done, and praying that, though he deserved to die himself, the death of his sacrifice might be accepted for the expiating of his guilt.

debates.question: What do the words rendered of his own voluntary will mean?

sides.position: To gain himself acceptance before the Lord: all the versions took it so and the connection requires it
That he may be accepted before the Lord — and the phrase for your acceptance goes with burnt and peace offerings, never with sin offerings
Ainsworth's reading, not the principle but the end of offering; though what pleases God must also be done by no constraint but love
On the received text it restricts the law to freewill offerings, which seems improper, since these rules governed the others too

debates.question: One hand or two on the victim's head?

sides.position: The Targum says the right hand, but the Jewish writers generally say both, with all his strength and nothing between his hands and the beast
Both hands, between the two horns, while the animal was alive, and no proxy could do it
Both hands, with all his might, between the horns
The verb implies a forcible pressure; the rite is named wherever the ceremonial is detailed and omitted wherever it is condensed

outliers.note: Alone sets the rite beside the heathen world, observing that almost every nation had burnt offerings and held the gods could be appeased no other way, some going as far as human sacrifice on the maxim that only a life redeems a life.

Alone preserves the words of confession said over the victim during the second Temple: I have sinned, I have committed iniquity, I have transgressed, but I repent before thee, and this is my atonement.

5.pericope_label: And he shall kill the bullock before the Lord: and the priests, Aaron's sons, shall bring the blood, and sprinkle the blood round about upon the altar that is by the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. And he shall flay the burnt offering, and cut it into his pieces. And the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire upon the altar, and lay the wood in order upon the fire: And the priests, Aaron's sons, shall lay the parts, the head, and the fat, in order upon the wood that is on the fire which is upon the altar: But his inwards and his legs shall he wash in water: and the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the Lord.

schools.summary: Settle who does what, because the chapter leaves it to the verbs. The laying on of hands was followed by the slaughtering, which was performed by the offerer himself in the case of the private sacrifices, and by the priests and Levites in that of the national and festal offerings. The sacrificer slaughtered the victim on the north side of the altar by cutting its throat, while a priest or an assistant held a bowl under the neck to receive the blood; before the Lord and before the door of the tent of meeting are two phrases which constantly interchange in these directions. Render the next verb throw rather than sprinkle. The priestly functions begin with the catching of the blood in the bowl and continue here: the priest threw the blood upon the walls of the altar in two portions, stepping first to the north-eastern corner and from it diffusing the blood over the northern and eastern walls, then placing himself at the south-western corner and from it diffusing the second portion over the southern and western; the rest he poured out at the southern side of the altar, which was furnished with two holes communicating with a drain that carried the blood into the Kedron. Then the sacrificer himself skinned and cut up the victim into its natural limbs, according to the separate joints, and was not to mangle it; the skin was the perquisite of the officiating priest. On the fire, confine the command to its occasion: the priests are to put fire upon the altar because they offered the sacrifice upon it, but this applies only to the first burnt offering presented after the erection of the altar, since afterwards the fire was always burning and was never allowed to go out. Add the rules for the fuel: no other than wood was allowed, no one might bring it from his own house but it had to be the wood of the congregation, and it had to be of the best kind, worm-eaten wood and timber from pulled-down buildings being excluded. On the laying of the pieces, render it lay the pieces in order, and note that the priests were not to place them upon the altar anyhow but to arrange them systematically, whence the rule obtained during the second Temple that the parts of the victim should as far as possible be arranged in the same order they occupied in the animal when alive. Define the washing precisely: the term for the inner parts here means the intestines of the abdomen, the stomach and bowels, and not those of the breast such as the lungs, heart and liver, since where the fat enveloping those is placed on the altar no washing is spoken of; and the cleansing had to be repeated three times before the ablution was deemed complete. Finally, mark the word for burning, which is not the one generally used of consuming by fire but originally signifies to make a fume or vapour by incense, the idea conveyed being that man upon earth fitly brought his gift to God in heaven by causing the odour of the burning sacrifice to ascend in a sweet-smelling savour.

Make the ministry of the priest the point of the whole passage. It was not allowable for a private person to kill the victim with his own hands; the priest was to prepare the victim itself and to pour its blood upon the altar, and what the priest did in their name was transferred to them. Draw the doctrine from the arrangement: although they brought the pledge of reconciliation from their own home, the ministers of expiation were to be sought elsewhere, since no one was competent for so illustrious an office save he who was graced by the holy unction of God. It was therefore plainly manifested that all mortals are unworthy of coming near God to propitiate him, and that the hands of all are in a manner polluted or profane except those which God himself has purged, since the honour of sacrificing came from nowhere else but from the grace of the Spirit. Then descend to the details as the traditions give them, and be honest where they conflict. On the killing, note that by the traditions of the elders it was valid when done by strangers, by women, by servants and even by unclean persons, provided the unclean did not touch the flesh, and that the service of the priest is said to begin only in the following clause; that the Targum makes the killer the butcher, that Aben Ezra interprets it of the priests, and that the Greek version renders it in the plural, they shall kill. On the flaying, observe that this was the only part of the victim not burnt and was the property of the priest; that the verb is singular and seems to mean the bringer of the offering, since the sons of Aaron who sprinkled the blood are spoken of in the plural; that Gersom holds the flaying and cutting in pieces lawful to a stranger while Aben Ezra reads it of the priest; and that the rule was that they do not flay the sacrifices until the blood is sprinkled. On the fire, record that it originally came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifice as a token of God's acceptance and was kept burning continually, yet that Jarchi, Maimonides and the Talmud agree that it was commanded to bring fire from a common place as well; and that this belonged to the priesthood and not the flaying or the cutting in pieces. On the washing, give the place and the manner, first in the room of the washers in the court and then upon the marble tables between the pillars, three times at least, and in water only, not in wine nor in a mixture of wine and water nor in any other liquid. Then read the whole typically: the killing before the Lord of the death of Christ, the flaying of his very great sufferings, the fire of the wrath of God revealed from heaven against all unrighteousness, and the washing of the internal purity of his heart and the external holiness of his life, and of the saints' purification by him in heart and life alike.

Take the ambiguity of the pronoun first and resolve it charitably. He that kills may be either the offerer, who is said to do it because he causes it to be done, men being commonly said to do what they cause others to do; or the priest, as the text goes on to say; or the Levite, whose office this was. On the blood, note that it was sprinkled in a considerable quantity, and that it signified both that the offerer deserved to have his own blood spilt in that manner, and that the blood of Christ should be poured forth for sinners, this being the only means of their reconciliation to God and acceptance with him. On the flaying, allow the probability that the person who brought the sacrifice killed, flayed, cut up and washed it, and then presented the parts and the blood to the priest, that he might burn the one and sprinkle the other; but grant it certain that the priests also, and the Levites, flayed the victims, and that the priest had the skin to himself. Note the one exception, that the red heifer alone was not flayed, but the whole body with the skin consumed by fire. On the fire, be strict: it was the fire that came out of the tabernacle from before the Lord and was kept perpetually burning, and it was not lawful to use any other fire in the service of God, as the case of Nadab and Abihu shows. Read the command accordingly as disposing rather than kindling, that is, blowing the fire up and putting it together so that it might be fit for the present work. Then describe the dividing of the sacrifice according to its larger joints: after the blood was poured out and the skin removed, the head was cut off; the caul which invests the intestines was taken out; the intestines with the mesentery were taken out and washed well, as also the fat; the four quarters were placed upon the altar and covered with the fat, the remains of the intestines laid upon them and the head above all; and then the sacred fire was applied and the whole mass consumed, which is the holocaust or complete burnt offering. Explain why the fat was gathered together, namely to increase the flame and consume the other parts more speedily. And close upon the savour. The phrase is a fire-offering, an odour of rest, or as the Greek expresses it a sacrifice for a sweet-smelling savour, which the apostle evidently had in view when he wrote that Christ loved us and gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice for a sweet-smelling savour, using the very same terms; whence the burnt offering typified the sacrifice and death of Christ for the sins of the world. Add the caution that the savour was not sweet in itself, for the burning rather caused a stink, but only as it represented that offering.

sides.position: The offerer in private sacrifices, the priests and Levites in the national and festal ones
The sacrificer himself, cutting the throat while a priest holds the bowl
Apparently the bringer, since no other is yet named and the traditions allow strangers, women, servants and the unclean; but the Targum says the butcher and Aben Ezra the priest
Not the offerer at all: no private person might kill the victim with his own hands, and what the priest did in their name was transferred to them
Either, since men are commonly said to do what they cause others to do

debates.question: What is meant by putting fire on the altar?

sides.position: The command applies only to the first offering on the newly erected altar, since afterwards the fire never went out
It was the fire that came from before the Lord and was kept perpetually burning; no other fire was lawful, as Nadab and Abihu show
Disposing rather than kindling — blowing the existing fire up and putting it together for the work
The rabbis held that though fire came down from heaven, fire was still commanded to be brought from a common place

outliers.note: Alone makes the priest's monopoly the doctrine of the passage: the pledge of reconciliation might be brought from home, but the ministers of expiation had to be sought elsewhere, all hands being polluted except those God himself has purged.
Alone reports Philo's mystical reading of the washing, that the inwards signified lusts to be washed away and the feet that we should walk no more on earth but mount through the air to heaven.

10.pericope_label: And if his offering be of the flocks, namely, of the sheep, or of the goats, for a burnt sacrifice; he shall bring it a male without blemish. And he shall kill it on the side of the altar northward before the Lord: and the priests, Aaron's sons, shall sprinkle his blood round about upon the altar. And he shall cut it into his pieces, with his head and his fat: and the priest shall lay them in order on the wood that is on the fire which is upon the altar: But he shall wash the inwards and the legs with water: and the priest shall bring it all, and burn it upon the altar: it is a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the Lord.

schools.summary: Say first why the section exists and then why it is short. Bullocks could of course only be offered by the wealthy, and the law now provides for those who could not afford so costly a sacrifice: they are to bring a lamb of the first year, which was the ordinary burnt offering in the time of Christ, and not a goat. The directions given for the burnt offering from bullocks apply equally to the burnt offering from the flock, and are therefore not repeated; the instructions already given for the oxen held good here, so that only the leading points are restated, together with a more precise description of the place of slaughtering. Explain that place on practical grounds and leave it there. The victim was killed by the side of the altar northward, that is, on the north side of the altar, and this was the rule with all the slain offerings, though it is stated only in connection with the burnt offerings, sin offerings and trespass offerings. The reason is simply the arrangement of the court: the place for the refuse was on the east side, the laver stood on the west side, and the ascent to the altar was on the south side, so that the north side was the most convenient for slaughtering the victims. Then stop on the grammar of the next verse, which the English obscures. The clause rendered with his head and his fat should be read, he shall cut it into its pieces, and sever or cut off its head and its fat; for by a figure of speech not uncommon in Hebrew one verb is connected with two substantives although it properly applies to only one of them, and a kindred verb has to be supplied for the second substantive to obtain the proper sense. Note in passing that the word rendered fat is used only in connection with the burnt offering, and signifies, according to the ancient versions and the rabbinical writers, those portions of fat which were separated from the entrails and taken out to be washed.

Treat the section as the repetition it is, and spend the space on the one new circumstance. Note that the flock might be brought as it might, and that the cutting into pieces and the washing of the inwards and the legs were done in the same manner as with the bullock, so that nothing needs to be said of them again. But the killing on the side of the altar northward is a circumstance not mentioned in the killing of the bullock, and it is worth the measurements. Maimonides describes a square place reaching from the wall of the altar northward to the wall of the court, sixty cubits, and all that was over against the breadth of this, from the wall of the porch to the eastern wall, seventy-six cubits; and this foursquare place is called the north, for the slaying of the most holy things, so that it seems this being a large place was fittest for the purpose. Then record the other explanation without adopting it outright. Aben Ezra intimates that some respect was had to the situation of Mount Zion, glossing the phrase as meaning without, and so the sides of the north, and correcting those who mistakenly place the tower of Zion in the midst of Jerusalem. With this agrees the note of Ainsworth, that hereby was figured that Christ our sin offering should be killed by the priests in Jerusalem and Mount Zion, which was on the sides of the north, and crucified on Mount Calvary. Keep the two explanations distinct, the one practical and the other typical, and do not let the second displace the first.

Where the law repeats itself, do not repeat with it; refer the reader back to the notes on the earlier verses for what is offered and for the cutting into pieces, and give the space to the one thing that is new. Here, on the north side, this and other kinds of sacrifices were killed, and the reason seems to be simply that here was the largest and most convenient place for the work, the altar being probably near the middle of the east end of the building and the entrance being on the south side. Having given the practical reason, add the typical one, but keep them in that order. This detail might also design the place of Christ's death, both more generally in Jerusalem, which the psalm places on the sides of the north, and more specially on Mount Calvary, which was on the north-west side of Jerusalem. Then draw the moral of the whole graded scale of victims, since this is where it becomes visible: the burnt offering may be a bullock, or a sheep or goat, or a bird, and the law descends deliberately from the costly to the cheap so that no worshipper is shut out. Note that the creatures named throughout are the mild and gentle ones, easily got and harmless, which is why they serve at once for the poor man's means and for a representation of the meekness of Christ. And keep the reading rule of the book in view even in a section of mere repetition: the sacrificial system exists to point out the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and the differences of price among the victims are not differences in what they signify.

Set the three grades of offering side by side, since that is what this section makes plain. Those of the middle rank, who could not well afford to offer a bullock, would bring a sheep or a goat; and those who were not able to do even that should be accepted of God if they brought a turtle-dove or a pigeon: for God, in his law and in his gospel, as well as in his providence, considers the poor. Observe next which creatures were chosen, namely those that were most mild and gentle, harmless and inoffensive, to typify the innocence and meekness that were in Christ and to teach the innocence and meekness that should be in Christians. On the place of slaughtering, guess practically and then allow yourself an image: perhaps on that side of the altar there was the largest vacant space, and room for the priests to turn themselves in; and it was of old observed that fair weather comes out of the north and that the north wind drives away rain, so that by these sacrifices the storms of God's wrath are scattered and the light of God's countenance is obtained, which is more pleasant than the brightest fairest weather. Then press the question of proportion on the reader, which is the real use of the passage. The offering of the poor was as typical of Christ's atonement as the more costly sacrifices, and expressed as fully repentance, faith and devotedness to God, since God accepts according to what a man hath and not according to what he hath not. But we can no more offer the sacrifice of a broken heart, or of praise and thanksgiving, than an Israelite could offer a bullock or a goat, except as God hath first given to us; and the more we do in the Lord's service, the greater are our obligations to him for the will, for the ability and for the opportunity. In many things God leaves us to fix what shall be spent in his service, whether of our time or our substance; yet where God's providence has put much into a man's power, scanty offerings will not be accepted, for they are not proper expressions of a willing mind.

debates.question: Why is the victim killed on the north side of the altar?

sides.position: Topography: the refuse lay east, the laver stood west and the ascent was south, leaving the north the only convenient side
Space: Maimonides measures a square of sixty cubits there, called the north, reserved for slaying the most holy things
Space, and then type — it may also mark the place of Christ's death, in Jerusalem and on Calvary
The largest vacant space, with room for the priests to turn in; and fair weather comes out of the north, as by these sacrifices God's wrath is scattered

outliers.note: Alone turns the north side into a figure from the weather, recalling that fair weather was said to come out of the north and the north wind to drive away rain, as by these sacrifices the storms of God's wrath are scattered.

Alone stops on the grammar of the twelfth verse, where one Hebrew verb governs two nouns though it suits only one, so that a second verb must be supplied: he shall cut it into its pieces, and sever its head and its fat.

14.pericope_label: And if the burnt sacrifice for his offering to the Lord be of fowls, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves, or of young pigeons. And the priest shall bring it unto the altar, and wring off his head, and burn it on the altar; and the blood thereof shall be wrung out at the side of the altar: And he shall pluck away his crop with his feathers, and cast it beside the altar on the east part, by the place of the ashes: And he shall cleave it with the wings thereof, but shall not divide it asunder: and the priest shall burn it upon the altar, upon the wood that is upon the fire: it is a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the Lord.

schools.summary: Begin with the classification. The fowls here stand in contrast to the cattle of the second verse, and just as the quadrupeds there were immediately defined to consist of bullocks, sheep and goats, so the generic term winged creature is here restricted to the dove and the pigeon; it will thus be seen that five different kinds are allowed for the burnt offering, the bullock, lamb, goat, dove and pigeon, the same that Abram was commanded to offer. Note that although in the burnt offering, as in the sin offering, pigeons were permitted to those too poor to offer quadrupeds, in certain other cases birds were prescribed for all irrespective of their circumstances. Account for the supply: turtledoves regularly came in large flocks into Palestine at certain periods, and the Israelites have reared pigeons and kept dovecots from time immemorial, a pursuit which continued a favourite with the later Jews, so that dealers in these birds sat with them in cages on stalls in the Temple court. Then explain the change of agent, which is the striking feature of the section. It was probably out of consideration for the feelings of the poor offerer, and to increase the importance of an otherwise small offering, that the priest himself brought the victim to the altar and slew it, instead of the worshipper performing these acts as in the case of quadrupeds; and the imposition of hands was dispensed with, both because the bird was too small for that ceremony and because the offerer brought it in his hands to the place of sacrifice, thus conveying by that act the idea involved in the imposition of hands. Describe the killing exactly: the priest is to use no knife but to nip off the head with his nails, to throw the severed head on the altar fire, and, since the small quantity of blood could not be caught in a bowl and would not suffice for throwing on the four walls, to press it out from the headless body and let it run down. On the crop, state the difficulty and both solutions. The obscure words probably mean its crop with the foeces thereof, following the Targum, where the Greek and Luther give the crop with its feathers, though the Hebrew for that would have been another word, and in any case if the crop were taken out the intestines with their contents would unquestionably come out along with it. Against that, the natural sense of the context is that as the skin was flayed from the quadruped so the feathers were removed from the bird before its body was placed on the fire, since one can hardly imagine victims burnt with the feathers and causing an intolerable smell; the marginal rendering with the filth thereof is now adopted by the greater number of expositors, and as the two words for filth and feathers resemble each other in Hebrew, it is probable that one of them has dropped out of the text. Conclude with the cleaving: before placing it on the fire the priest made an incision in the wings without separating them wholly from the body, corresponding in some degree to the limbing of the quadruped.

Take the bird as the offering of the poorest sort, who could offer neither a bullock nor a sheep nor a lamb, and then follow the ceremony closely, since almost every clause has a Jewish gloss worth recording. The priest brought it to the altar, that is, to the south-east horn of it, near which was the place of the ashes, into which the crop and its feathers were cast. On the crop, note that the phrase may be rendered with its meat, or with its dung, as Onkelos has it, meaning that which was in the crop; that the Jerusalem Targum interprets it with its dung, and Jonathan's paraphrase with its collection, that is, what was gathered together in the crop; and that Gersom observes it includes the entrails. On the cleaving, describe it exactly: one wing being on one side and the other on the other, the body of the bird was cleaved down the middle and yet not parted asunder, nor was any of its wings separated from it, which the Targum of Jonathan renders, but shall not separate its wings from it. Then read the detail, and let it carry the weight of the chapter's close. This denoted that though by the death of Christ his soul and body were separated from each other, the human nature was not separated from his divine Person, the personal union between the two natures still continuing; nor was he divided from his divine Father, for though he was forsaken by him he was still in union with him as the Son of God; nor from the divine Spirit, by which he offered up himself to God and by which he was quickened; nor from his church and people, for whom he suffered, they being united to him as members to their head. Finish by noting that the priest burnt it upon the altar in like manner as the ox, the sheep or the goat were burnt.

Explain the choice of birds before the ceremony. These were appointed for the poor who could not bring better, and they are preferred before others partly because they were easily gotten and partly because they are fit representations of Christ's chastity, meekness and gentleness, for which these birds are remarkable. Mark the one distinction of age: the pigeons must be young, because then they are best, but the turtledoves are better when they are grown up, and are therefore not confined to that age. Then set out the sequence of the sacrifice: the head was violently wrung off, then the blood was poured out, then the feathers were plucked off, the breast was cut open, the crop, stomach and intestines were taken out, and then the body was burnt; and though the bird was split up, it was not divided asunder. Guard a possible confusion here: the head was severed from the rest of the body, as sufficiently appears because it was to be burnt by itself and the body afterwards, and the direction elsewhere that he shall wring the head from the neck but not divide it asunder is spoken not of the burnt offering but of the sin offering. On the refuse, note that with its feathers may mean with its dung or filth, contained in the crop and in the guts, and that it was cast on the east of the tabernacle because this was the remotest place from the holy of holies, which was at the west end; and teach from it that impure things and persons should not presume to approach to God, but should be banished from his presence. Then gather up the whole chapter, since this is its last section. Four kinds of animals might be made burnt offerings, and all must be without spot or blemish, the most perfect of their respective kinds, and wholly consumed by fire; the rich were to bring the most costly and the poor those of least price. See how much mercy was mingled even in this requisition of justice: if a man could not bring a bullock or a heifer, a goat or a sheep, let him bring a calf, a kid or a lamb; if he could not bring any of these because of his poverty, let him bring a turtle-dove or a young pigeon; and in cases of extreme poverty even a little fine flour was accepted by the bountiful Lord as a sufficient oblation, which brought the benefits of the sacrificial service within the reach of the poorest of the poor. And close where the chapter's own logic closes, that after all this, to love God with all our heart and to love our neighbour as ourselves is better than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.

debates.question: Does he pluck away the crop with the feathers or with the filth?

sides.position: With the filth: the Targums render it the dung or what was gathered in the crop, and Gersom includes the entrails
With the filth: the Greek and Luther give feathers but the Hebrew would need another word, and the intestines come away with the crop in any case

The feathers, by the sense of the context, since the birds can hardly have been burnt feathered; but most expositors now prefer the filth, and two similar Hebrew words have probably collapsed into one
The dung or filth contained in the crop and guts

debates.question: Why does the priest, not the offerer, handle this sacrifice?

sides.position: Out of consideration for a poor offerer's feelings, and to give a small offering weight; the laying on of hands was dispensed with because he had carried the bird in his own hands
The text simply assigns the acts to the priest, who brings it to the south-east horn where the ashes lay
The grading of victims is itself the mercy: where a man could not reach a bird, even fine flour was accepted

outliers.note: Alone reads the rule that the bird be cleft but not parted as a figure of the unbroken union of Christ's person: his soul and body were separated in death, but the human nature was not divided from the divine Person, nor he from the Father who forsook him.
Alone explains the trade in birds, that because of these sacrifices the Jews kept dovecots and reared pigeons, so that dealers sat with cages of them on stalls in the Temple court.
